Ich habe lange auf diese Gelegenheit gewartet. (I've been waiting a long time for this opportunity.)
Verb 'warten' + auf + accusative.exceptions:
EXCEPTIONS AND VARIATIONS:

1. 'WARTEN MIT' (different meaning): to wait with/delay something
   - Ich warte mit dem Essen. (I'm delaying the meal.)
   - NOT the same as 'warten auf'!

2. 'ABWARTEN' (separable verb): to wait and see
   - Wir müssen abwarten. (We have to wait and see.)
   - Das bleibt abzuwarten. (That remains to be seen.)

3. WITHOUT PREPOSITION (rare, meaning 'to maintain/service'):
   - Die Techniker warten die Maschinen. (The technicians service the machines.)
   - Completely different meaning!

4. ERWARTEN (inseparable, no preposition): to expect
   - Ich erwarte dich um 8 Uhr. (I expect you at 8 o'clock.)
   - NOT: erwarten auf

5. FIGURATIVE USE: 'warten auf' can be used for things metaphorically waiting
   - Zu Hause wartet eine Überraschung auf uns. (A surprise awaits us at home.)
   - Das Buch wartet darauf, dass du es abholst. (The book is waiting for you to pick it up.)

6. OLD/FORMAL: Genitive case (veraltet)
   - Dort wartete ihrer eine Überraschung. (A surprise awaited them there.)
   - This form is archaic and rarely used

Future expressed with present tense.explanation_en: German commonly uses the present tense (Präsens) for future events when context (time expressions, dates, adverbs) makes the future meaning clear. This is preferred over 'werden + infinitive' when certainty is high: 'Ich bleibe bis Sonntag' (I will stay until Sunday). The future tense with 'werden' is reserved for predictions, intentions, or when future isn't clear from context.
Future expressed with present tense.full_rule:
PRESENT TENSE FOR FUTURE MEANING:

1. WHEN TO USE PRESENT FOR FUTURE:
   The present tense expresses future when:
   a) Time expressions make it clear: heute Abend, morgen, nächste Woche, 2027
   b) The action is planned/scheduled with high certainty
   c) Questions about plans: Wie lange bleibst du? (How long will you stay?)
   
   Structure: PRESENT TENSE + TIME EXPRESSION
   - Ich bleibe bis Sonntag. (I will stay until Sunday.)
   - Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin. (Tomorrow I'm going/will go to Berlin.)
   - 2027 fahre ich nach Kolumbien. (In 2027 I'm going to Colombia.)
   - Nächste Woche fängt die Schule an. (School starts next week.)

2. COMMON TIME EXPRESSIONS FOR FUTURE:
   - morgen (tomorrow)
   - übermorgen (day after tomorrow)
   - heute Abend (this evening)
   - nächste Woche/nächsten Monat/nächstes Jahr
   - in zwei Tagen (in two days)
   - bald (soon)
   - später (later)
   - gleich (right away/soon)

3. WHEN TO USE 'WERDEN' + INFINITIVE (FUTUR I):
   a) Predictions/uncertainty: Es wird regnen. (It will rain.)
   b) Promises/intentions: Ich werde dir helfen. (I will help you.)
   c) Assumptions about present: Er wird wohl krank sein. (He's probably sick.)
   d) When no time marker makes future clear
   
   Structure: werden (conjugated) + INFINITIVE (end)
   - Es wird schneien. (It will snow.)
   - Ich werde ein neues Auto kaufen. (I will buy a new car.)

4. CONJUGATION OF 'WERDEN' (Futur I):
   ich werde ... bleiben
   du wirst ... bleiben
   er/sie/es wird ... bleiben
   wir werden ... bleiben
   ihr werdet ... bleiben
   sie/Sie werden ... bleiben

5. PRESENT VS. FUTUR I COMPARISON:
   CERTAIN/PLANNED → Present:
   - Ich fahre morgen nach München. (I'm going to Munich tomorrow.)
   
   INTENTION/PROMISE → Futur I:
   - Ich werde nach München fahren. (I will go to Munich. - promise/intention)

6. QUESTIONS ABOUT FUTURE:
   Usually present tense is used:
   - Kommst du morgen? (Are you coming tomorrow?)
   - Wie lange bleibst du hier? (How long will you stay here?)
   - Wann fährt der Zug ab? (When does/will the train leave?)
Future expressed with present tense.common_mistakes:
ITALIAN SPEAKERS' COMMON ERRORS:

1. OVERUSING FUTURE TENSE: Italian uses future tense ('andrò') more often; German prefers present
   ❌ Ich werde bis Sonntag bleiben (too formal for simple future)
   ✓ Ich bleibe bis Sonntag (natural German)
   Compare Italian: 'Resterò fino a domenica' (future tense normal)

2. FORGETTING TIME MARKERS: Using present without clear future context
   ❌ Ich fahre nach Kolumbien (unclear when - could be now)
   ✓ Ich fahre 2027 nach Kolumbien (clear future time)
   ✓ Ich fahre morgen nach Kolumbien

3. WRONG WORD ORDER WITH 'WERDEN':
   ❌ Ich werde fahren morgen nach Berlin (infinitive must be at end)
   ✓ Ich werde morgen nach Berlin fahren

4. CONFUSING 'WERDEN' = 'TO BECOME' WITH FUTURE:
   ❌ Ich werde müde (I'm becoming tired - NOT future!)
   ✓ Ich werde müde sein (I will be tired - future)

5. USING FUTURE FOR SCHEDULED EVENTS: Germans prefer present for schedules
   ❌ Der Zug wird um 9 Uhr ankommen (sounds like uncertainty)
   ✓ Der Zug kommt um 9 Uhr an (schedule - certain)

6. LITERAL TRANSLATION OF ITALIAN PRESENT CONTINUOUS:
   Italian: 'Sto per partire' (I'm about to leave)
   ❌ Ich bin zu fahren (doesn't exist)
   ✓ Ich fahre gleich (I'm leaving soon)
   ✓ Ich bin dabei zu fahren (I'm in the process of leaving - rare)
examples: Wie lange bleibst du hier? (How long will you stay here?)
Ich bleibe bis Sonntag. (I will stay until Sunday.)
2027 fahre ich nach Kolumbien. (In 2027 I'm going to Colombia.)
Morgen gehe ich ins Kino. (Tomorrow I'm going to the cinema.)
Future expressed with present tense.exceptions:
EXCEPTIONS AND SPECIAL CASES:

1. MODAL VERBS: Often use 'werden' even with time expressions for nuance
   - Ich werde morgen kommen müssen. (I will have to come tomorrow. - emphasis on obligation)
   - vs. Ich muss morgen kommen. (I have to come tomorrow. - simpler)

2. WEATHER PREDICTIONS: Usually require 'werden'
   - Es wird morgen regnen. (It will rain tomorrow. - prediction)
   - NOT: Es regnet morgen (sounds strange)

3. IMMEDIATE FUTURE: 'gleich' with present is very common
   - Ich komme gleich. (I'm coming right away.)
   - Der Bus kommt gleich. (The bus is coming soon.)

4. 'WERDEN' FOR ASSUMPTIONS ABOUT PRESENT:
   - Er wird wohl krank sein. (He's probably sick. - NOT future!)
   - Sie wird im Büro sein. (She's probably in the office.)

5. FUTUR II (rare): Used for assumptions about past
   - Er wird wohl angekommen sein. (He has probably arrived.)
   - Structure: werden + past participle + sein/haben

6. FIXED SCHEDULES: Always present tense
   - Der Film beginnt um 20 Uhr. (The movie starts at 8 PM.)
   - Die Schule fängt am Montag an. (School starts on Monday.)
   - Das Konzert findet nächste Woche statt. (The concert takes place next week.)

7. 'WOLLEN' VS. 'WERDEN' FOR INTENTION:
   - Ich will nach Berlin fahren. (I want to go to Berlin. - desire)
   - Ich werde nach Berlin fahren. (I will go to Berlin. - promise/determination)

Perfekt with sein: schon im Urlaub gewes.rule: Perfekt with sein: schon im Urlaub gewesen
Perfekt with sein: schon im Urlaub gewes.explanation_en: To say you have already been on a trip, German uses the Perfekt tense with the auxiliary 'sein' plus 'gewesen' (past participle of sein). 'Du bist schon im Urlaub gewesen' = 'You have already been on vacation.'
Perfekt with sein: schon im Urlaub gewes.full_rule:
sein is one of the handful of verbs (along with passieren, bleiben, werden) that always form the Perfekt with the auxiliary sein rather than haben. Because sein is both the main verb and its own auxiliary here, the Perfekt of sein looks like 'sein (conjugated) + gewesen'.

CONJUGATION TABLE - Perfekt of 'sein' (Duden):
ich bin gewesen
du bist gewesen
er/sie/es ist gewesen
wir sind gewesen
ihr seid gewesen
sie/Sie sind gewesen

Plusquamperfekt (for reference): ich war gewesen, du warst gewesen, er/sie/es war gewesen, wir waren gewesen, ihr wart gewesen, sie waren gewesen.

General rule for haben vs sein in the Perfekt (germanveryeasy.com / Duden):
- sein is used as the auxiliary for: the verbs sein, passieren, bleiben, werden; intransitive verbs of movement/change of location (gehen, fahren, laufen, rennen, springen, fallen, kommen, fliegen, schwimmen); intransitive verbs expressing a change of state (sterben, werden, aufwachen, einschlafen, wachsen, schmelzen).
- haben is used in all other cases (transitive verbs, reflexive verbs, most intransitive verbs that don't express motion/change of state).
- Some motion verbs (schwimmen, joggen, klettern, tanzen) can take either haben or sein depending on whether the focus is on the activity itself (haben) or on covering a distance/reaching a destination (sein).

Word order note: with time expressions like 'schon' (already), the adverb is placed directly after the conjugated auxiliary: Subject + sein(conj.) + schon + [place phrase] + gewesen. E.g. 'Du bist schon im Urlaub gewesen.'
Perfekt with sein: schon im Urlaub gewes.common_mistakes: Italian speakers, whose L1 Perfetto Composto also uses two auxiliaries (essere/avere), sometimes still default to using 'haben' for 'sein' or confuse it with the Italian pattern 'essere stato/a', and try to add a gender/number-agreeing ending onto 'gewesen' (German past participles used with an auxiliary do NOT agree in gender/number, unlike Italian past participles with essere, e.g. 'sono stata/stato'). Another common error is placing 'gewesen' in the wrong position: Italian word order keeps the participle right after the auxiliary ('sono stata a casa'), so learners may say '*Ich bin gewesen schon im Urlaub' instead of correctly sending the participle 'gewesen' to the very end of the clause: 'Ich bin schon im Urlaub gewesen.' Learners also sometimes confuse 'sein' (to be) with 'sein' as a possessive pronoun (his/its), leading to confusion when parsing sentences with 'ist gewesen'.
examples: Du bist schon im Urlaub gewesen.
Ich bin gestern wieder zurück nach Hause gekommen.
Wir sind noch nie in Italien gewesen.
Seid ihr schon einmal in Berlin gewesen?
Perfekt with sein: schon im Urlaub gewes.exceptions: A small set of verbs (liegen, sitzen, stehen) form the Perfekt with 'haben' in northern Germany but with 'sein' in southern Germany, Austria, and Switzerland (regional variation confirmed by Duden: 'Ich habe gelegen/gestanden/gesessen' vs. 'Ich bin gelegen/gestanden/gesessen'). Motion verbs like schwimmen, fahren, fliegen, klettern, joggen can take either haben or sein depending on whether the emphasis is on the action/duration (haben) or the movement/destination (sein). The verbs gehen and reisen are now used almost exclusively with sein in modern German.

gerade in Nebensätzen (subordinate claus.explanation_en: When using 'gerade' (right now, currently) in a subordinate clause introduced by 'weil', the word order is: subordinating conjunction + subject + gerade + rest of verb phrase, with the conjugated verb at the end.
gerade in Nebensätzen (subordinate claus.full_rule:
German subordinate clauses (Nebensätze) introduced by a subordinating conjunction such as weil, dass, wenn, ob, obwohl, etc. send the conjugated (finite) verb to the very end of the clause. Word order pattern for weil-clauses containing 'gerade':
weil + subject + (time/gerade) + object(s)/other adverbials + non-finite verb parts + conjugated verb (end)

This follows the general TeKaMoLo principle (Temporal-Kausal-Modal-Lokal) for ordering middle-field elements, with 'gerade' functioning as a temporal adverb placed early in the clause, directly after the subject (and after any pronoun objects), but before the rest of the verb phrase (objects, separable prefixes, or infinitives), with the conjugated verb pushed to the final position.

Structure: Hauptsatz, weil + Subjekt + gerade + (Objekt/e) + Verb (finit, am Ende).
Example structure: 'Ich habe keine Zeit, weil ich gerade meine Wohnung putze.' -> weil (conj.) + ich (subj.) + gerade (adv.) + meine Wohnung (obj.) + putze (finite verb, end).

This mirrors the general subordinate-clause rule: a subordinating conjunction kicks the conjugated verb to the end of its clause, and the word order within the clause otherwise remains similar to a main clause (subject, objects, adverbials), just without the verb in second position.
gerade in Nebensätzen (subordinate claus.common_mistakes: Kevin tended to place 'gerade' incorrectly or overcomplicate the sentence structure instead of using this simple pattern. Italian speakers commonly struggle with this rule because Italian subordinate clauses (e.g., 'perché sto pulendo la mia casa proprio ora') keep the verb in second position, right after the subject, with adverbs like 'proprio ora'/'adesso' typically placed at the end or beginning of the clause, never forcing the verb to the clause-final position. This leads Italian learners to build sentences like '*weil ich putze gerade meine Wohnung' (keeping the verb in 'normal' second position, as in a main clause) instead of correctly moving 'putze' to the end: 'weil ich gerade meine Wohnung putze.' A second frequent error is forgetting the comma before 'weil', since Italian 'perché' does not obligatorily require comma separation in the same systematic way. Italian speakers may also over-complicate the sentence by trying to front 'gerade' at the very start of the clause (as they might with 'proprio ora' in Italian), producing incorrect orders such as '*weil gerade ich meine Wohnung putze.'
examples: Ich habe keine Zeit, weil ich gerade meine Wohnung putze.
Sie sind im Flugzeug, weil sie gerade in den Urlaub fahren.
Er geht nicht ans Telefon, weil er gerade duscht.
Wir können nicht sprechen, weil wir gerade das Abendessen kochen.
gerade in Nebensätzen (subordinate claus.exceptions: The coordinating conjunction 'denn' (also meaning 'because') does NOT trigger verb-final word order — unlike 'weil', a clause with 'denn' keeps normal main-clause (verb-second) word order, so 'gerade' in a denn-clause behaves like in any main clause: 'Ich habe keine Zeit, denn ich putze gerade meine Wohnung.' In colloquial spoken German, some native speakers use 'weil' informally with main-clause (verb-second) word order ('weil ich putze gerade...'), but this is considered non-standard and should be avoided in formal or written German. When a modal verb or Perfekt tense is involved, 'gerade' still occupies the same early position in the middle field, while it is the auxiliary/modal verb (not the participle or infinitive) that moves to the clause-final position.

wütend auf + Akkusativ.explanation_en: The adjective 'wütend' (angry) is used with the preposition 'auf', which requires the accusative case here, not the dative.
wütend auf + Akkusativ.full_rule:
'auf' belongs to the group of nine German two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen) that can take either the accusative or the dative case depending on meaning (motion/direction -> accusative; static location -> dative). However, when 'auf' is used figuratively/idiomatically after certain adjectives of emotion — such as 'wütend auf' (angry at), 'stolz auf' (proud of), 'eifersüchtig auf' (jealous of), 'gespannt auf' (curious about) — it is fixed and always governs the ACCUSATIVE case, regardless of any physical motion or location.

DECLENSION TABLE for 'auf' + Akkusativ (masculine/feminine/neuter/plural):
auf + den (masc.) - wütend auf den Mann
auf + die (fem.) - wütend auf die Frau
auf + das (neut.) - wütend auf das Kind
auf + die (plural) - wütend auf die Leute
Contraction: auf + das = aufs (less common with this idiom)

Duden confirms the idiomatic phrase 'wütend auf/über jemanden sein' (to be very angry/incensed), listing 'auf' as a standard preposition choice alongside 'über' for this meaning. A commonly cited nuance (from general usage sources) is that 'wütend auf' + Akkusativ is typically used with a person as the object of anger, while 'wütend über' + Akkusativ is used with a thing, statement, or situation as the cause of anger.
wütend auf + Akkusativ.common_mistakes: Kevin initially tried 'über' with dative; corrected to 'auf' + accusative. Italian speakers frequently make this error because the equivalent Italian construction 'arrabbiato con qualcuno' uses 'con' (with), which has no case-marking equivalent in Italian, so learners have no built-in intuition for which German case to select and often default to the dative because many two-way prepositions describing static 'location of emotion' seem, by analogy with physical location (e.g., 'im Zimmer'), to call for dative. Another typical error is mixing up 'auf' and 'über': because Italian uses a single preposition regardless of whether the object of anger is a person or a situation, Italian learners often use 'wütend über' even when referring to a person, or vice versa. Learners also sometimes wrongly decline the noun after 'auf' in the dative (e.g., '*wütend auf der Frau' instead of correctly 'wütend auf die Frau'), treating 'auf' as always requiring dative because of its frequent use in fixed dative expressions like 'auf der Arbeit'.
examples: Er ist wütend auf die Frau.
Ich bin wütend auf meinen Bruder.
Warum bist du so wütend auf mich?
Sie war wütend auf ihren Kollegen, weil er zu spät kam.
wütend auf + Akkusativ.exceptions: 'wütend über' + Akkusativ is an accepted alternative, generally used when the cause of the anger is a thing, statement, or situation rather than a person (e.g., 'Er war wütend über die ungerechte Behandlung' — angry about the unjust treatment), whereas 'wütend auf' is preferred with a person as the object. As a two-way preposition, 'auf' still takes the dative in its literal, spatial sense of static location (e.g., 'Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch' — the book lies on the table), so learners must distinguish the fixed idiomatic emotional use (always accusative) from the general locative use (dative for location, accusative for motion onto a surface).

durch + Akkusativ.explanation_en: The preposition 'durch' (meaning 'through' or 'by means of') always governs the accusative case, regardless of the verb or context in the sentence.
durch + Akkusativ.full_rule:
Declension of definite/indefinite articles after 'durch' (Akkusativ):
Masculine: durch den Park, durch einen Park
Feminine: durch die Stadt, durch eine Stadt
Neuter: durch das Haus, durch ein Haus
Plural: durch die Straßen

Personal pronouns after 'durch' (Akkusativ):
durch mich, durch dich, durch ihn, durch sie, durch es, durch uns, durch euch, durch sie, durch Sie

'Durch' is one of the fixed accusative prepositions, grouped with: für, ohne, gegen, um, entlang (postpositive) — often remembered by the mnemonic 'FUDGO' or similar acronyms.
durch + Akkusativ.common_mistakes: Italian speakers, whose language does not mark case on articles, often incorrectly apply dative forms after 'durch' by analogy with other prepositions they've learned (e.g., saying 'durch dem Park' instead of 'durch den Park'), confusing it with dative-triggering prepositions like 'mit' or 'nach'. Another common mistake is failing to decline the article at all, using the base form regardless of gender/case.
examples: Sie geht durch den Park.
Wir fahren durch die Stadt.
Das Licht scheint durch das Fenster.
Er hat den Erfolg durch harte Arbeit erreicht.
durch + Akkusativ.exceptions: No true exceptions exist to the rule that 'durch' takes accusative; it is one of the fixed accusative prepositions in German with no dative or genitive usage. However, in certain fixed idiomatic expressions ('durch und durch' = 'through and through'), no article is used, so case marking is not visibly tested.

Separable verbs: rausschauen, reinschaue.rule: Separable verbs: rausschauen, reinschauen, reingehen, rausgehen
Separable verbs: rausschauen, reinschaue.explanation_en: These are separable verbs formed from the colloquial short prefixes 'raus' (contraction of 'heraus', meaning 'out') and 'rein' (contraction of 'herein', meaning 'in') combined with base verbs like 'schauen' (to look) or 'gehen' (to go). As separable verbs, the prefix detaches and moves to the end of the clause in finite main-clause constructions, while staying joined in the infinitive.
Separable verbs: rausschauen, reinschaue.full_rule:
Conjugation of 'rausschauen' (to look out), present tense:
ich schaue raus
du schaust raus
er/sie/es schaut raus
wir schauen raus
ihr schaut raus
sie/Sie schauen raus

Conjugation of 'reingehen' (to go in), present tense:
ich gehe rein
du gehst rein
er/sie/es geht rein
wir gehen rein
ihr geht rein
sie/Sie gehen rein

Imperative forms:
Schau raus! (Look out! - informal singular)
Schaut raus! (Look out! - informal plural)
Schauen Sie raus! (Look out! - formal)
Geh rein! / Geht rein! / Gehen Sie rein!

Note: 'raus' and 'rein' are colloquial shortenings of the full literary forms 'heraus' (out, toward speaker) and 'hinein' (in, away from speaker); 'herein' (in, toward speaker) and 'hinaus' (out, away from speaker) also exist. In casual speech, 'raus' and 'rein' are used regardless of direction relative to speaker, though formally the distinction persists (e.g., 'herausschauen' vs. 'hinausschauen').
Separable verbs: rausschauen, reinschaue.common_mistakes: Italian speakers often fail to separate the prefix in conjugated forms, incorrectly saying 'Ich rausschaue' instead of 'Ich schaue raus', by analogy with Italian verbs which do not split. They also frequently confuse 'raus' and 'rein' with directionality errors, or forget that formal German distinguishes 'her-' (toward speaker) and 'hin-' (away from speaker) compounds, oversimplifying by using only 'raus/rein' in contexts requiring more precision in writing.
examples: Die Frau links schaut raus.
Schau rein, bevor du reingehst!
Wir gehen jetzt raus, es ist schön draußen.
Er schaut oft aus dem Fenster raus.
Separable verbs: rausschauen, reinschaue.exceptions: In formal or written German, the fuller forms 'heraus-', 'hinaus-', 'herein-', 'hinein-' are preferred over the colloquial 'raus-'/'rein-' shortenings (e.g., 'hinausgehen' instead of 'rausgehen'). Additionally, when used with certain verbs, these prefixes may carry idiomatic meanings not directly translating literal 'in/out' motion (e.g., 'rauskommen' can mean 'to come out/result' in abstract contexts, not just literal exit).

wegen + Genitiv (colloquial: Dativ).explanation_en: The preposition 'wegen' (because of, due to) is a genitive preposition in standard German and requires the noun following it to be in the genitive case. However, in everyday spoken German, it is extremely common to hear 'wegen' followed by the dative case instead, especially with plural nouns or nouns without a strong genitive marker. Duden and grammar authorities note that dative use is widespread colloquially but is still considered non-standard in formal writing.
wegen + Genitiv (colloquial: Dativ).full_rule:
STANDARD (GENITIVE) USE:
wegen + genitive noun phrase

Genitive articles/determiners:
- Masculine: des (+ -s/-es on noun) — wegen des Regens
- Feminine: der — wegen der Schule
- Neuter: des (+ -s/-es on noun) — wegen des Wetters
- Plural: der — wegen der Kinder

Full declension table (definite article, genitive):
| Gender | Genitive Article | Example |
|--------|------------------|---------|
| Masculine | des + noun-(e)s | wegen des Autos |
| Feminine | der | wegen der Arbeit |
| Neuter | des + noun-(e)s | wegen des Geldes |
| Plural | der | wegen der Leute |

COLLOQUIAL (DATIVE) USE:
wegen + dative noun phrase (common in spoken German)

| Gender | Dative Article | Example |
|--------|-----------------|---------|
| Masculine | dem | wegen dem Auto |
| Feminine | der | wegen der Schule (same as genitive) |
| Neuter | dem | wegen dem Geld |
| Plural | den (+ -n on noun) | wegen den Leuten |

With personal pronouns, 'wegen' typically combines with possessive-based forms: wegen mir, wegen dir, wegen ihm, wegen ihr, wegen uns, wegen euch, wegen ihnen (dative-based, very common even in fairly formal speech, though 'meinetwegen', 'deinetwegen', 'seinetwegen', 'ihretwegen', 'unseretwegen', 'euretwegen', 'ihretwegen' are the prescriptively correct fused forms).

With proper names, 'wegen' + name generally takes no article and looks the same in both cases: wegen Nico, wegen Maria.
wegen + Genitiv (colloquial: Dativ).common_mistakes: Italian speakers often struggle because Italian has no case system, so the concept of choosing between genitive and dative after a preposition is unfamiliar. Common errors include: (1) using nominative forms after 'wegen' by direct word-for-word translation from Italian 'a causa di + noun' (e.g., incorrectly saying 'wegen der Mann' instead of 'wegen des Mannes' or colloquial 'wegen dem Mann'); (2) forgetting the genitive -s/-es ending on masculine/neuter nouns (e.g., saying 'wegen des Auto' instead of 'wegen des Autos'); (3) not realizing that dative is acceptable colloquially, leading learners to either avoid 'wegen' or overcorrect awkwardly; (4) confusing 'wegen' with 'weil' (because), since Italian 'perché' covers both 'why' and 'because', causing learners to use 'wegen' with a full clause instead of a noun phrase (wegen + noun vs. weil + subordinate clause).
examples: Es war wegen der Schule.
Wegen dem Auto (colloquial) / Wegen des Autos (formal).
Sie sind wütend wegen Nico.
Wegen des schlechten Wetters mussten wir zu Hause bleiben.
Wegen dir bin ich zu spät gekommen. (colloquial, dative-based)
wegen + Genitiv (colloquial: Dativ).exceptions: With feminine singular nouns, the genitive and dative articles are identical ('der'), so there is no visible difference between formal and colloquial usage (e.g., 'wegen der Schule' works for both). With personal pronouns, the fused genitive forms (meinetwegen, deinetwegen, etc.) are traditionally preferred in correct written German, though 'wegen mir/dir/ihm' is very common in speech. With plural nouns lacking a genitive -n ending marker, colloquial dative plural (wegen den Leuten) is extremely frequent even among educated speakers. Duden explicitly acknowledges the genitive as standard but recognizes the dative as a widely tolerated colloquial variant, particularly when the genitive would be ambiguous or the noun has no case ending (e.g., 'wegen Geschäften' vs. dative clarity).

als vs. immer wenn (subordinate clauses.rule: als vs. immer wenn (subordinate clauses of time)
als vs. immer wenn (subordinate clauses.explanation_en: 'Als' is used for a single, one-time event in the past. 'Immer wenn' (or just 'wenn' referring to repeated past events) is used for repeated/habitual events in the past. 'Wenn' alone is used for present/future single or repeated events.
examples: Als wir geheiratet haben, haben wir eine große Party gemacht.
Immer wenn es geregnet hat, bin ich zu Hause geblieben.
Wenn wir heiraten, machen wir eine große Party.
als vs. immer wenn (subordinate clauses.common_mistakes: Using 'wenn' instead of 'als' for single past events.

Separable verbs: anfangen and aufhören.explanation_en: 'Anfangen' (to begin/start) and 'aufhören' (to stop/cease) are separable-prefix verbs (trennbare Verben) in German. Their prefixes 'an-' and 'auf-' detach from the verb stem and move to the final position in present tense and simple past main clauses. In the perfect tense, the prefix reattaches to the front of the past participle, with 'ge-' inserted between the prefix and the stem.
Separable verbs: anfangen and aufhören.full_rule:
CONJUGATION OF 'ANFANGEN' (to begin) — Present Tense:
| Pronoun | Form |
|---------|------|
| ich | fange an |
| du | fängst an |
| er/sie/es | fängt an |
| wir | fangen an |
| ihr | fangt an |
| sie/Sie | fangen an |

Simple Past (Präteritum):
| Pronoun | Form |
|---------|------|
| ich | fing an |
| du | fingst an |
| er/sie/es | fing an |
| wir | fingen an |
| ihr | fingt an |
| sie/Sie | fingen an |

Perfect Tense: hat/haben + angefangen (past participle: an + ge + fangen)
Example: Ich habe angefangen.

CONJUGATION OF 'AUFHÖREN' (to stop) — Present Tense:
| Pronoun | Form |
|---------|------|
| ich | höre auf |
| du | hörst auf |
| er/sie/es | hört auf |
| wir | hören auf |
| ihr | hört auf |
| sie/Sie | hören auf |

Simple Past (Präteritum):
| Pronoun | Form |
|---------|------|
| ich | hörte auf |
| du | hörtest auf |
| er/sie/es | hörte auf |
| wir | hörten auf |
| ihr | hörtet auf |
| sie/Sie | hörten auf |

Perfect Tense: hat/haben + aufgehört (past participle: auf + ge + hört)
Example: Du hast aufgehört.

WORD ORDER RULES:
- Main clause, present/simple past: conjugated verb in position 2, separable prefix at the end.
  Example: Ich fange die Arbeit morgen an.
- Subordinate clause: verb + prefix reunite at the end, prefix attaches directly before the conjugated verb.
  Example: ..., weil ich die Arbeit morgen anfange.
- Perfect tense: auxiliary (haben) in position 2, past participle (with prefix+ge+stem) at the end.
  Example: Ich habe die Arbeit angefangen.
- Modal verb constructions: modal verb conjugated in position 2, infinitive (with prefix attached, not separated) at the end.
  Example: Du darfst nie aufhören. / Ich muss jetzt anfangen.
Separable verbs: anfangen and aufhören.common_mistakes: Italian speakers, whose language has no separable verb prefixes, commonly make these errors: (1) forgetting to split the prefix in main clauses and instead keeping it attached like an infinitive (e.g., incorrectly saying 'Ich anfange die Arbeit' instead of 'Ich fange die Arbeit an'); (2) placing the separated prefix in the wrong position, not at the very end of the clause; (3) forgetting to insert 'ge-' between the prefix and stem in the past participle (e.g., saying 'geanfangen' instead of 'angefangen', or omitting it entirely as 'anfangen' instead of 'angefangen'); (4) with modal verb constructions, incorrectly separating the prefix when it should remain attached to the infinitive at the end (e.g., saying 'Du darfst nie auf hören' as two separate final elements incorrectly ordered, instead of 'Du darfst nie aufhören'); (5) confusing which auxiliary verb to use in the perfect tense (both use 'haben', but Italian speakers sometimes default to 'sein' by analogy with Italian intransitive verbs of motion/change like 'cominciare' patterns).
examples: Ich habe die Arbeit vor zwei Jahren angefangen.
Du darfst nie aufhören.
Der Unterricht fängt um acht Uhr an.
Wann hörst du mit der Arbeit auf?
Separable verbs: anfangen and aufhören.exceptions: When 'anfangen' or 'aufhören' are used with a dependent infinitive construction using 'zu' (e.g., 'aufhören zu rauchen' - to stop smoking), the prefix still separates in main clause conjugated forms, but the 'zu' is inserted between the prefix and stem of the second (dependent) infinitive verb, not of anfangen/aufhören itself: 'Er hört auf zu rauchen' (correct - prefix of aufhören separates; 'zu' belongs to rauchen). In subordinate clauses, verbs remain unseparated and moved to clause-final position: 'Ich weiß, dass er aufhört.' Additionally, in constructions with modal verbs, the separable verb stays as one infinitive unit and is NOT split: 'Er will anfangen' (not 'Er will an fangen').

Perfect tense formation with regular and.rule: Perfect tense formation with regular and irregular verbs
Perfect tense formation with regular and.explanation_en: The Perfekt (present perfect) tense in German is formed with a conjugated auxiliary verb (haben or sein) in second position plus a past participle at the end of the clause. Regular (weak) verbs form participles with ge-...-t, while irregular (strong) verbs typically form participles with ge-...-en and often a stem vowel change. This tense is commonly used in spoken German and informal writing to describe past events, including work history narratives.
Perfect tense formation with regular and.full_rule:
REGULAR (WEAK) VERB PARTICIPLE FORMATION:
ge + stem + t
Example: arbeiten → gearbeitet; machen → gemacht; kündigen → gekündigt

IRREGULAR (STRONG) VERB PARTICIPLE FORMATION:
ge + (often changed) stem + en
Example: enden → geendet (actually weak/regular); nehmen → genommen; sprechen → gesprochen

Note: 'entlassen' (to lay off/dismiss) is a strong verb with an inseparable prefix 'ent-', so it does NOT take 'ge-' in the participle: entlassen → entlassen (participle identical to infinitive, following the rule that verbs with inseparable prefixes be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-, miss- omit 'ge-').

AUXILIARY VERB SELECTION:
- Most transitive verbs and verbs describing activities use 'haben': ich habe gearbeitet, sie haben entlassen.
- Verbs of motion/change of state typically use 'sein': ich bin gegangen (not relevant to the given examples, but a key contrast).

FULL CONJUGATION TABLE — PERFEKT with 'haben' (example verb: arbeiten):
| Pronoun | Form |
|---------|------|
| ich | habe gearbeitet |
| du | hast gearbeitet |
| er/sie/es | hat gearbeitet |
| wir | haben gearbeitet |
| ihr | habt gearbeitet |
| sie/Sie | haben gearbeitet |

RELEVANT VERB PARTICIPLES FROM WORK-HISTORY CONTEXT:
| Infinitive | Participle | Type |
|------------|------------|------|
| arbeiten | gearbeitet | regular/weak |
| anfangen | angefangen | strong, separable |
| kündigen | gekündigt | regular/weak |
| entlassen | entlassen | strong, inseparable prefix (no ge-) |
| enden | geendet | regular/weak |

WORD ORDER: Subject + auxiliary (position 2) + ... + past participle (final position).
Example: Ich habe acht Jahre lang in der Chemie-Industrie gearbeitet.
Perfect tense formation with regular and.common_mistakes: Italian speakers frequently make these errors: (1) direct translation of time expressions from Italian/English word order, placing time phrases at the end of the sentence (e.g., 'Ich habe gearbeitet acht Jahre lang' instead of the correct 'Ich habe acht Jahre lang gearbeitet'), since German requires the past participle to remain in final position with time expressions inserted in the middle (following the 'Zeit-Manner-Ort' / time-manner-place rule known as TeKaMoLo); (2) incorrectly adding 'ge-' to verbs with inseparable prefixes like 'entlassen', producing the incorrect 'geentlassen' instead of correct 'entlassen'; (3) choosing the wrong auxiliary verb, especially defaulting to 'sein' by analogy with Italian's 'essere' for certain verbs (Italian uses 'essere' more broadly than German uses 'sein'); (4) confusing weak/strong verb participle patterns, e.g., adding '-t' to strong verbs or '-en' to weak verbs; (5) mispositioning the auxiliary verb, since Italian avere/essere + participle typically stay adjacent, while German requires the participle to move to the very end of the clause, potentially far from the auxiliary.
examples: Ich habe acht Jahre lang in der Chemie-Industrie gearbeitet.
Sie haben fünfzig Prozent des Personals entlassen.
Der Vertrag hat im Februar geendet.
Ich habe im letzten Jahr gekündigt, weil ich unzufrieden war.
Perfect tense formation with regular and.exceptions: Verbs with inseparable prefixes (be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-, miss-) do not add 'ge-' in the participle (e.g., entlassen → entlassen, verstehen → verstanden). Verbs ending in -ieren also do not take 'ge-' in the participle (e.g., studieren → studiert, telefonieren → telefoniert). Separable verbs insert '-ge-' between the prefix and the stem (e.g., anfangen → angefangen, as covered in the separable verb rule). A small number of verbs are 'mixed' (weak conjugation with a vowel change), such as denken → gedacht, bringen → gebracht, which don't fit neatly into either the fully regular or fully irregular pattern.

Time expressions: vor + Dativ (ago).explanation_en: The preposition 'vor' followed by a dative-case time expression is used in German to express the English concept of 'ago' (e.g., 'two years ago' = 'vor zwei Jahren'). Unlike English, where 'ago' follows the time period at the end of a phrase, German 'vor' precedes the time expression and functions grammatically like other prepositional phrases, meaning it follows standard German word order rules (often appearing in the middle of the sentence, in the time-manner-place slot) rather than being fixed at the sentence's end.
Time expressions: vor + Dativ (ago).full_rule:
STRUCTURE: vor + dative time expression

'Vor' is a two-way (Wechselpräposition) preposition that takes dative case when indicating a temporal or static spatial relationship (as opposed to accusative for directional movement). In time expressions meaning 'ago', it always takes the dative.

DATIVE CASE ENDINGS FOR TIME EXPRESSIONS (with plural nouns, most common in 'ago' phrases):
| Article/Determiner | Dative Plural Form |
|---------------------|---------------------|
| die (plural def. article) | den (+ -n on noun) |
| meine, seine, ihre, etc. | meinen, seinen, ihren (+ -n on noun) |
| zwei, drei, etc. (no article) | zwei, drei + noun with -n ending |

EXAMPLES OF DECLENSION:
- vor einem Jahr (dative singular, neuter: 'Jahr')
- vor einer Woche (dative singular, feminine: 'Woche')
- vor zwei Jahren (dative plural: 'Jahre' → 'Jahren')
- vor drei Monaten (dative plural: 'Monate' → 'Monaten')
- vor fünf Minuten (dative plural: 'Minuten', already ends in -n)

WORD ORDER: In German main clauses, 'vor + time' phrases typically appear after the conjugated verb but can shift position depending on emphasis, following the general TeKaMoLo (Temporal-Kausal-Modal-Lokal) guideline for placing adverbial information. It is NOT fixed at the end of the sentence as 'ago' is in English.

Correct: Ich habe die Arbeit vor zwei Jahren angefangen.
(Literal gloss: I have the work before-two-years begun.)

Incorrect (English-influenced): Ich habe die Arbeit angefangen vor zwei Jahren.
Time expressions: vor + Dativ (ago).common_mistakes: Italian speakers (and English speakers) commonly make these errors: (1) placing 'vor + time' at the very end of the sentence, mirroring English 'ago' placement or Italian 'fa' placement (Italian: 'due anni fa' also places the time expression at the end), producing incorrect German like 'Ich habe die Arbeit angefangen vor zwei Jahren' instead of correct 'Ich habe die Arbeit vor zwei Jahren angefangen'; (2) forgetting to decline the noun into dative case, especially forgetting the plural dative -n ending (e.g., saying 'vor zwei Jahre' instead of 'vor zwei Jahren'); (3) confusing 'vor' (ago, referring to past time from now) with 'seit' (since, referring to a duration that continues into the present) — Italian 'da' can cover meanings similar to both, leading to confusion between vor + Perfekt/Präteritum vs. seit + Präsens; (4) using accusative instead of dative after 'vor' by incorrectly treating it as a directional (movement) preposition rather than a static/temporal one.
examples: Es war vor zwei Jahren.
Ich habe die Arbeit vor zwei Jahren angefangen.
Vor einem Monat habe ich gekündigt.
Wir haben uns vor drei Wochen kennengelernt.
Time expressions: vor + Dativ (ago).exceptions: When emphasis is desired, 'vor + time' can be moved to the very first position in the sentence (position 1), causing subject-verb inversion, which is grammatically correct and common for emphasis: 'Vor zwei Jahren habe ich die Arbeit angefangen.' This is different from placing it at the end, which remains incorrect. Additionally, 'vor' should not be confused with 'seit' + dative, which is used for actions/states that began in the past and continue into the present (typically paired with present tense in German, unlike English's present perfect continuous): 'Ich arbeite seit zwei Jahren hier' (I have been working here for two years) versus 'Ich habe vor zwei Jahren hier gearbeitet' (I worked here two years ago, completed action).

Strong verbs: no vowel change in the ihr.rule: Strong verbs: no vowel change in the ihr form
Strong verbs: no vowel change in the ihr.explanation_en: Strong (irregular) verbs that alter their stem vowel do so ONLY in the du and er/sie/es forms of the present tense. In the ich, wir, ihr and sie/Sie forms the vowel stays in its base (infinitive) form. Thus: ihr fahrt (not fährt), ihr esst (not isst), ihr lest (not liest). Even native speakers occasionally slip and write 'Ihr fährt', but this is an error.
Strong verbs: no vowel change in the ihr.full_rule:
Stem-changing (strong) verbs shift the vowel only in 2nd/3rd person singular. Four change classes:

a -> ä (fahren): ich fahre | du fährst | er/sie/es fährt | wir fahren | ihr fahrt | sie/Sie fahren
e -> i (essen): ich esse | du isst | er isst | wir essen | ihr esst | sie essen
e -> ie (lesen): ich lese | du liest | er liest | wir lesen | ihr lest | sie lesen
au -> äu (laufen): ich laufe | du läufst | er läuft | wir laufen | ihr lauft | sie laufen

Ending spelling for the ihr form depends on the stem final consonant: stems ending in -s/-ss/-ß/-z take just -t (ihr esst, ihr lest, ihr heißt, ihr sitzt); stems ending in -t/-d take -et (ihr haltet, ihr ratet, ihr findet). Note: modal verbs behave oppositely - they change in the singular but KEEP the changed/umlaut form in plural: ihr könnt, ihr müsst, ihr dürft, ihr wisst. Irregular: ihr seid (sein).
Strong verbs: no vowel change in the ihr.common_mistakes: Italian dittongazione (e.g. sedere: io siedo, tu siedi, lui siede, noi sediamo, voi sedete, loro siedono) changes the vowel in 1sg and 3pl too. So Italian speakers wrongly extend the umlaut/vowel change to those persons: *ich fähre, *sie fähren, *wir essen->*wir issen. The voi form (sedete) actually matches German ihr correctly. Italian speakers also confuse the -s stem ending (*ihr esset). Because Italian polite 'Voi' overlaps with 'ihr', learners may use ihr where Sie is required.
examples: Wohin fahrt ihr nach dem Gardasee?
Wo esst ihr normalerweise zu Mittag?
Warum lauft ihr so schnell? - Ihr lauft ja wie die Profis!
Lest ihr abends noch Bücher, oder seht ihr lieber fern?
Strong verbs: no vowel change in the ihr.exceptions: The du-imperative reveals a split: e->i/ie verbs KEEP the vowel change and drop the -e (Iss!, Nimm!, Lies!, Sieh!), but a->ä and au->äu verbs do NOT umlaut in the imperative (Fahr!, Lauf!, Halt! - never *Fähr!). The ihr-imperative is identical to the ihr present form (Fahrt!, Esst!, Lest!). Modal verbs invert the pattern (umlaut kept in plural: ihr könnt, ihr müsst). Sein is irregular throughout (ihr seid, not *seit).

Question words: wo, woher, wohin.explanation_en: wo = where (location), woher = where from (origin), wohin = where to (direction). Use them at the start of a question with the verb in second position.
examples: Woher kommt ihr?
Wohin fahrt ihr nach dem Gardasee?
Wo esst ihr normalerweise?

einander + preposition.explanation_en: The reciprocal pronoun 'einander' (each other/one another) combines with a preposition to form a single, invariable lowercase word: miteinander (with each other), untereinander (among each other), füreinander (for each other), voneinander (from each other). The preposition's case is absorbed into the fixed compound, so einander itself never declines.
einander + preposition.full_rule: The productive reciprocal compounds: aneinander, aufeinander, auseinander, beieinander, durcheinander, füreinander, gegeneinander, hintereinander, ineinander, miteinander, nacheinander, nebeneinander, übereinander, umeinander, untereinander, voneinander, voreinander, zueinander. Each is written as ONE word, lowercase, and is indeclinable. Reason it is obligatory: bare reflexive 'sich' can express reciprocity on its own (Sie waschen sich = they wash each other/themselves), BUT sich cannot be the object of a preposition in a reciprocal sense - *Sie sprechen mit sich is wrong; German therefore requires the fused prepositional form: Sie sprechen miteinander. With a separable-style verb the compound still stands apart from the verb: Wir warten aufeinander. Note: 'einander gegenüber' is conventionally written as two words (sie sitzen einander gegenüber), not as a single compound.
einander + preposition.common_mistakes: Italian expresses reciprocity with reflexive 'si' or 'l'un l'altro'/'tra loro'. Italian speakers therefore (1) split the spelling as a calque of 'l'un l'altro': *mit einander, *für einander; (2) use *unter ihnen for 'untereinander' (from 'tra loro') or *mit sich for 'miteinander' (from 'parlano con sé'); (3) reach for 'zusammen' where a reciprocal meaning is required; (4) try to decline einander.
examples: Sie sprechen nur untereinander.
Sie reden kaum miteinander.
Die beiden Kinder haben viel Verständnis füreinander.
Nach dem Streit haben sie tagelang nichts voneinander gehört.
einander + preposition.exceptions: Several compounds are lexicalized and no longer purely reciprocal: auseinander (apart), durcheinander (in a muddle/confused), nacheinander and hintereinander (one after another, in sequence). 'untereinander' can also mean physically 'one below the other'. There is no genitive reciprocal form - use 'gegenseitig' instead (gegenseitiges Vertrauen). 'einander gegenüber' stays as two words.

Direction toward water: an + accusative.explanation_en: 'an' is a two-way (Wechsel) preposition. To express movement/direction TOWARD a shoreline or body of water (wohin?), use 'an' + accusative: an die Adria, ans Meer. For static location (wo?), use 'an' + dative: an der Adria, am Meer. Watch the gender of the water noun, since it determines the article form.
Direction toward water: an + accusative.full_rule:
Direction (wohin? - accusative) vs. Location (wo? - dative):
Wir fahren an die Adria. | Wir sind an der Adria.
Wir fahren ans Meer. | Wir sind am Meer.
Wir fahren an den Strand. | Wir liegen am Strand.
Wir fahren an den See. | Wir wohnen am See.
Contractions: an + das = ans; an + dem = am.

Genders: das Meer, die See (= the sea), but DER See (= lake); der Strand, die Küste, das Ufer, der Fluss, der Ozean. Named waters: die Adria, die Nordsee, die Ostsee, die Karibik, das Mittelmeer, der Atlantik, der Bodensee, der Rhein, die Donau, die Mosel.
Direction toward water: an + accusative.common_mistakes: Italian 'al mare' is ONE form for both direction and location, so the accusative/dative contrast is unmarked in the L1: Italian speakers produce both *Wir fahren am Meer (should be accusative) and *Wir sind ans Meer (should be dative). They also calque 'a' as *zum Meer instead of 'ans Meer'. Gender transfer causes errors: 'il mare' (masc) -> *an den Meer; 'l'Adriatico' (masc) -> *an den Adria; 'i Caraibi' (masc pl) -> the German is die Karibik (fem sg). 'in spiaggia' -> *in den Strand instead of 'an den Strand'.
examples: Wir fahren an die Adria.
Wir fahren ans Meer.
Im Sommer fahren wir jedes Jahr an die Ostsee.
Die Kinder rennen an den Strand und springen dann ins Meer.
Direction toward water: an + accusative.exceptions: Use 'in' + accusative for going INTO the water (ins Meer springen, ins Wasser gehen), as opposed to 'an' + accusative for going TO the shore. Use 'auf' + accusative for heading out ONTO the open water (aufs Meer hinausfahren). For islands and places used without an article, use 'nach' (nach Sylt, nach Rügen), but 'an die Nordsee' for the sea region; use 'auf die Insel' for going onto an island. The homograph der See (lake) vs. die See (sea) is the key gender trap.

wegen + Genitiv.explanation_en: 'wegen' (because of) takes the Genitive case. A 'weil'-clause can be rewritten with 'wegen' + a Genitive noun phrase.
examples: Wegen des schlechten Wetters bleibe ich zu Hause.
Wegen des Alkohols kann ich nicht schlafen.
Wegen seiner schlechten Ernährung hat er ein schwaches Immunsystem.

Genitiv: article and noun forms.explanation_en: Genitive articles: des (masc./neut.), der (fem./plural). Masculine and neuter nouns add -(e)s: des Mannes, des Kindes. Feminine and plural nouns stay unchanged: der Frau, der Kunden.
Genitiv: article and noun forms.full_rule:
Definite article (Genitive):
Masc: des | Fem: der | Neut: des | Plural: der

Indefinite/possessive (ein-/mein-):
Masc: eines/meines | Fem: einer/meiner | Neut: eines/meines | Plural: (keiner/meiner)

Noun endings:
- Masc./Neut. add -s or -es: des Autos, des Mannes, des Kindes.
- -es is obligatory after -s, -ß, -x, -z, -tsch: des Hauses, des Platzes, des Reflexes. Nouns in -nis double the s: des Ergebnisses.
- Fem. and plural nouns do NOT change: der Frau, der Kunden, der Meetings.
- N-declension masculines take -(e)n, not -s: des Kunden, des Studenten, des Jungen, des Menschen. Mixed: des Namens, des Herzens, des Gedankens.
Genitiv: article and noun forms.common_mistakes: Italian uses 'di + article' for possession and has no case system, so speakers often replace the Genitive with 'von + Dativ' (*die Betreuung von den Kunden instead of die Betreuung der Kunden). They also drop the -(e)s on masc./neut. nouns (*des Mann, *des Kind) and wrongly add -s to feminine nouns (*der Fraus). N-declension endings are frequently forgotten (*des Kunds instead of des Kunden).
examples: die Betreuung der Kunden
die Planung der Meetings
die Erledigung des Schriftverkehrs
das Auto des Mannes
Genitiv: article and noun forms.exceptions: N-declension masculines end in -(e)n (des Studenten, des Kunden) rather than -s; a few mixed nouns add -ns (des Namens, des Herzens). Proper names normally take -s before the noun (Annas Buch, Peters Auto) and names ending in -s/-z use an apostrophe (Klaus' Auto). In spoken German 'von + Dativ' often replaces the Genitive.

Adjective endings in the Genitive.explanation_en: In the Genitive the adjective ending is usually -en (weak and mixed declensions), like the Dative. BUT in the strong (unpreceded) declension, feminine and plural take -er, so the 'always -en' rule is not universal.
Adjective endings in the Genitive.full_rule:
Genitive adjective endings by declension:

Weak (after der/die/das):
Masc: des guten Mannes | Fem: der guten Frau | Neut: des guten Kindes | Pl: der guten Kinder → all -en

Mixed (after ein/kein/mein):
Masc: eines guten Mannes | Fem: einer guten Frau | Neut: eines guten Kindes | Pl: keiner guten Kinder → all -en

Strong (no article):
Masc: guten Weines | Fem: großer Hitze | Neut: guten Wetters | Pl: kleiner Kinder
→ Masc./Neut. = -en, but Fem./Pl. = -er

So the input's 'always -en, like the Dative' holds only for weak/mixed and for strong masc./neut. It fails in the strong feminine and plural (genitive -er vs. dative -en: wegen kleiner Kinder / mit kleinen Kindern).
Adjective endings in the Genitive.common_mistakes: Italian marks adjectives only for gender and number, not case, so speakers fail to inflect for the Genitive (*wegen des schlechte Wetters instead of schlechten). They also over-apply the '-en everywhere' shortcut and write *wegen großen Hitze / *trotz schweren Verletzungen instead of the strong forms großer Hitze / schwerer Verletzungen.
examples: wegen des schlechten Wetters
wegen der gesättigten Fettsäuren
wegen seiner schlechten Ernährung
trotz schwerer Verletzungen
Adjective endings in the Genitive.exceptions: The unpreceded (strong) declension breaks the 'always -en' rule: feminine and plural take -er (wegen großer Hitze, die Rechte kleiner Kinder, trotz schwerer Verletzungen). Strong masculine and neuter, however, do end in -en (wegen schlechten Wetters), and the noun itself carries the -es ending.

mir tut ... weh (expressing pain).explanation_en: With wehtun the body part is the subject in the Nominative and the affected person is in the Dative. Normally you name what hurts, but an impersonal 'es' is also possible (Tut es weh?).
mir tut ... weh (expressing pain).full_rule:
Verb 'wehtun' (separable, dative object):
Present: es tut mir weh / dir / ihm / ihr / uns / euch / ihnen / Ihnen weh
Plural subject → plural verb: die Füße tun mir weh.
Perfect: es hat mir wehgetan.

Dative pronouns: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen.

Structure: [Nominative body part = subject] + tut/tun + [Dative person] + weh.
- Der Kopf tut mir weh.
- Die Beine tun mir weh.
Alternatively use the possessive without dative: Mein Kopf tut weh.
mir tut ... weh (expressing pain).common_mistakes: Italian 'mi fa male la testa' leads to two errors: (1) using the accusative because Italian 'mi' is case-ambiguous → *Es tut mich weh instead of Es tut mir weh; (2) combining possessive and dative → *Mein Kopf tut mir weh (say either Der Kopf tut mir weh OR Mein Kopf tut weh, not both). Italians also forget plural verb agreement: *Die Füße tut mir weh instead of tun.
examples: Der Nacken tut mir weh.
Was tut dir weh?
Mein Kopf tut weh.
Die Beine tun mir weh.
mir tut ... weh (expressing pain).exceptions: You do not always have to name the body part: an impersonal 'es' is fully idiomatic — Tut es weh?, Es tut weh, Wo tut es weh? Note also the figurative meaning 'to hurt emotionally': Deine Worte haben mir wehgetan.

Impersonal mir ist / mir wird + adjectiv.rule: Impersonal mir ist / mir wird + adjective
Impersonal mir ist / mir wird + adjectiv.explanation_en: For temperature and feeling unwell, German uses a Dative construction: mir ist kalt/warm/schlecht/schwindelig, and mir wird schlecht for a change of state. Exception: for tiredness you say 'ich bin müde', not 'mir ist müde'.
Impersonal mir ist / mir wird + adjectiv.full_rule:
sein + Dative (state) and werden + Dative (change of state):
mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen/Ihnen ist ... (kalt, warm, heiß, schlecht, übel, schwindelig, langweilig)
mir wird ... (schlecht, übel, schwindelig, warm) = becoming.

Dative-impersonal adjectives: kalt, warm, heiß, schlecht, übel, schwindelig, langweilig, peinlich, egal.
Nominative-only (use ich bin ...): müde, krank, hungrig, durstig, nervös.

Word order: Mir ist kalt / Es ist mir kalt. The 'es' is dropped when another element opens the sentence.
Impersonal mir ist / mir wird + adjectiv.common_mistakes: The signature Italian error copies 'ho freddo/caldo' (have cold/warm) → *Ich habe kalt / *Ich habe warm instead of Mir ist kalt/warm. Note 'Ich bin kalt' is grammatical but means 'I am cold-hearted'. From 'ho sonno/sono stanco' speakers may say *Mir ist müde instead of Ich bin müde, and from 'mi gira la testa' they may forget the dative (*Ich bin schwindelig instead of Mir ist schwindelig).
examples: Mir ist schlecht.
Mir wird schlecht vom Alkohol.
Mir ist schwindelig.
Ich bin müde.
Impersonal mir ist / mir wird + adjectiv.exceptions: Tiredness, hunger, thirst and illness use the Nominative with sein: ich bin müde/hungrig/durstig/krank, NOT *mir ist müde. Also, physical adjectives like groß/klein/dick only work with sein + Nominative (ich bin groß), never in the dative-impersonal pattern.
